items.prompt: A B-tree node that is not a leaf holds 3 keys. How many children does it have?
hints: A node with k keys that is not a leaf has k + 1 children.
3 keys make 4 gaps: before, between and after them, so 4 children.

options.feedback: There is one child before the first key and one after the last, so one more child than keys.
Each key does not have its own pair of children; neighbouring keys share the child between them.

items.prompt: In this tree, which child of the root would hold 33?
hints: Each child holds the keys between two neighbouring keys of its parent.
20 < 33 < 40, so 33 belongs in the middle child.

options.feedback: The first child holds keys smaller than 20.
The last child holds keys larger than 40.

items.prompt: Tap the nodes a search for 30 visits, from the root down.
Which statement about the keys inside one B-tree node is true?
hints: Think about how a search decides which child to follow.
Keys in a node are kept in order.
They are sorted, so each key separates the ranges of the subtrees beside it.

options.text: They are kept in sorted order
options.feedback: Yes. Sorted keys are what let a search pick the right child.

options.text: They can be in any order, because the children do the sorting
options.feedback: Without sorted keys, a search could not tell which child to follow.

options.text: Each node holds exactly one key
options.feedback: That is a binary search tree. B-tree nodes hold several keys.
